l: private revenge, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_justified_by the law [for crimes the law cannot touch] Private revenge is presented by Holmes as potentially justified when the law cannot touch certain crimes. He says his sympathies are with the criminals rather than Charles Milverton, whose killing avenges the harm caused by his blackmail.

l: Mr. Horace Harker, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Horace Harker is a journalist for the Central Press Syndicate living at 131 Pitt Street. He owns Napoleon busts, including one bought from Harding Brothers for his room. After hearing a disturbance and yell at night, he finds an unidentified murdered man outside and discovers his mantelpiece bust destroyed. He reports the events to Lestrade, Holmes, and Watson, then writes a sensational account calling it murder by a madman.

l: Morse Hudson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Morse Hudson, a small, stout picture-dealer, sold three of the six Napoleon busts, including two to Dr. Barnicot and one to Devine. After another bust was smashed in his shop, he identified Beppo as a former Italian piece-work employee.

l: Napoleon the First, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Napoleon the First, a French Emperor admired by Dr. Barnicot and represented by hundreds of London statues, becomes the target of systematically destroyed busts.

l: Harding Brothers, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Harding Brothers is a Kensington picture and sculpture retailer. It obtains three Napoleon busts from Gelder & Co. and sells all three, respectively to Horace Harker, Josiah Brown, and Mr. Sandeford; it also sells Devine’s last Napoleon bust to Sandeford.

l: Kennington Road, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Kennington Road contains Morse Hudson’s shop, where a Napoleon bust is destroyed, and Dr. Barnicot’s residence and consulting-room, later burgled; the stolen hall bust is carried into the garden and smashed against a wall.

l: Pitt Street, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Pitt Street contains Mr. Horace Harker’s house at 131, where an image-breaker removes a Napoleon bust and an unidentified man is murdered; Holmes finds the bust destroyed in a nearby empty house’s garden.

l: Napoleon bust, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: A plaster cast of Napoleon owned by Mr. Horace Harker is taken during a nighttime intrusion, then found smashed into fragments in the garden of an empty Campden House Road house.

l: Napoleon busts (Dr. Barnicot's collection), The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Dr. Barnicot owns two duplicate plaster casts of Devine's head of Napoleon, bought for his Kennington Road hall and Lower Brixton Road surgery. During separate nighttime intrusions, both busts are destroyed; they came from the same mould as the bust destroyed at Morse Hudson's shop.

l: Pietro Venucci, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Pietro Venucci is the murder victim found outside 131 Pitt Street in connection with the Kensington incident. Tall, sunburned, powerful, poorly dressed, apparently under thirty, and unidentified at first, he is found with his throat cut. A horn-handled clasp knife lies beside him, while his pocket holds a photograph of the dead man; an apple, string, and a shilling map are also found. He is later identified as Lucretia Venucci’s brother, a notorious Naples cut-throat allegedly connected to the Mafia. Lestrade and Holmes link his murder to Beppo and the pearl, but the exact relationship remains uncertain.

l: image-breaker, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: targets Napoleon bust [breaks busts rather than taking them] The image-breaker enters or approaches several premises to locate and destroy plaster busts of Napoleon the First. The person removes busts before breaking them when circumstances require, avoids darker locations, and may have been involved in the events at 131 Pitt Street.

l: Napoleon bust destruction series, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: A chain of incidents involving identical plaster busts of Napoleon begins with a bust destroyed at Morse Hudson's shop, continues through burglaries at Dr. Barnicot's residences, and reaches Horace Harker's house, where a bust's removal coincides with an unidentified man's murder.

l: burglary of Dr. Barnicot's residences, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Dr. Barnicot's Kennington Road residence is burgled, but the only item taken is the Napoleon bust from his hall, which is smashed in the garden. His Lower Brixton Road surgery is also entered, and the duplicate bust on the mantelpiece is smashed where it stood.

l: murder at 131 Pitt Street, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: A murder outside Horace Harker's 131 Pitt Street house occurs during an apparent attempt to remove his Napoleon bust; a dead man is found with his throat cut, and the murderer remains unidentified.

l: photograph of the dead man, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: depicts dead man (Pitt Street) [a sharp-featured, simian-looking man] A snapshot found in the dead man's possession shows an alert, sharp-featured simian man with thick eyebrows and a pronounced lower face resembling a baboon's muzzle. Holmes studies the photograph and keeps it temporarily with Lestrade's permission for further investigation.

l: Gelder & Co., The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Gelder & Co. is a Stepney wholesale manufacturer of sculpture works, producing Napoleon busts. It supplied three casts to Morse Hudson and three to Harding Brothers, the two halves of a batch of six made in two plaster moulds. The manager reported no known differences among the casts. Beppo worked there and, while the six busts dried in the passage, concealed the pearl in one of them.

l: Beppo, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Beppo is an Italian former sculptor, workman, and known criminal who worked for Gelder & Co. and formerly for Morse Hudson. Though considered a good worker and fluent in English, he earlier knifed another Italian at Gelder & Co., was arrested, and received a one-year sentence. Before that arrest, he hid the famous black pearl of the Borgias inside one of six wet plaster Napoleon busts. After imprisonment, he traces the dispersed busts across London and destroys them to recover the pearl. Holmes seeks him as the bust-breaker, and Beppo is captured at Laburnum Villa while smashing Josiah Brown’s bust, carrying a bloodstained long sheath knife.

l: Devine’s head of Napoleon, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Devine’s head of Napoleon was the marble original from which hundreds of plaster casts were made at Gelder & Co.

l: Napoleon busts, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Napoleon busts are plaster casts made from Devine’s head, formed from joined plaster profiles; several are destroyed, and Holmes expects Beppo to attack the remaining examples.

l: Morse Hudson’s three Napoleon busts, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Morse Hudson received three Napoleon busts from Gelder & Co.; two were sold to Dr. Barnicot, and the third was smashed on Hudson’s counter in broad daylight.

l: Harding Brothers’ three Napoleon busts, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: includes Napoleon busts [three casts] Harding Brothers received three Napoleon busts from Gelder & Co. They sold them to Horace Harker, Josiah Brown, and Mr. Sandeford; Brown’s bust is later broken by Beppo at Laburnum Villa.

l: photograph of Beppo, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The photograph is shown to Morse Hudson and the manager of Gelder & Co., who both identify the pictured man as Beppo. Holmes uses it to connect Beppo with the destroyed busts and with the man arrested at Laburnum Villa.

l: Josiah Brown, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Josiah Brown, owner of Laburnum Villa in Chiswick and a Harding Brothers Napoleon bust, receives Sherlock Holmes’s letter, locks his house, and waits inside while Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Inspector Lestrade watch outside.

l: Laburnum Villa, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: contains Napoleon busts [one bust targeted by Beppo] Laburnum Villa was Josiah Brown’s house in Chiswick and contained one of Harding Brothers’ remaining Napoleon busts. Beppo entered the house and broke the bust outside, where Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Inspector Lestrade arrested him.

l: Mr. Sandeford, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Mr. Sandeford of Reading owns Devine’s last Napoleon bust, having paid fifteen shillings, then brings it to Holmes and sells all rights for ten pounds.

l: evening newspaper, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: publishes Horace Harker newspaper account [highly sensational and flowery] The evening newspaper reported the Kensington incident under the headline “Kensington Outrage. Murder by a Madman.” It printed a sensational account and repeated the conclusion attributed to Inspector Lestrade and Sherlock Holmes that the events arose from lunacy rather than deliberate crime; Holmes also used it to plant a misleading clue for Beppo.

l: Mafia, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_a secret political society [enforces decrees by murder] The Mafia is described by Inspector Lestrade as a secret political society that enforces its decrees by murder. Lestrade believes Pietro Venucci was pursuing another Italian because that person had broken Mafia rules.

l: murder of Pietro Venucci, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The murder of Pietro Venucci was a fatal knife stabbing during Beppo’s search for the busts. Inspector Lestrade first attributed it to a struggle between Pietro and another Italian, possibly Beppo. Holmes later concludes that Pietro, Beppo’s confederate, confronted him at Harker’s over the lost pearl, and Beppo stabbed him in the scuffle.

l: destruction of the Napoleon busts, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The destruction affects busts sold through Morse Hudson and Harding Brothers, with Beppo connected to the incidents through his work at the relevant establishments. Holmes arranges surveillance at Laburnum Villa and catches Beppo breaking Josiah Brown’s bust, but his examination finds no visible peculiarity in the plaster fragments.

l: letter from Sherlock Holmes to Josiah Brown, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Sherlock Holmes sends Josiah Brown an urgent letter by express messenger. Brown follows its instructions by locking every door inside Laburnum Villa and awaiting the expected intruder, enabling Holmes and the others to catch Beppo.

l: Lucretia Venucci, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Lucretia Venucci, the Italian maid of the Princess and Pietro’s sister, is believed by Holmes to be connected to the pearl’s disappearance through Pietro and possibly Beppo.

l: Reading, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: contains Devine’s Napoleon bust [the final remaining bust] Reading is the location associated with Mr. Sandeford and the final surviving bust. Holmes determines that the Reading bust must contain the pearl after the other busts have been eliminated.

l: Devine’s Napoleon bust, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: contains the famous black pearl of the Borgias [the Reading specimen] Devine’s Napoleon bust is the type of plaster figure that Holmes seeks and that Gelder & Co. manufactured in a group of six. The last specimen, bought from Mr. Sandeford, contains the hidden pearl.

l: the famous black pearl of the Borgias, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The famous black pearl of the Borgias is recovered from inside the Reading Napoleon bust. Holmes identifies it as the valuable jewel that disappeared from the Prince of Colonna’s bedroom at the Dacre Hotel.

l: the disappearance of the Borgia pearl, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: At Prince of Colonna’s bedroom in the Dacre Hotel, the Borgia pearl disappears, causing a sensation; police initially fail to recover it, but Holmes eventually finds it inside a Napoleon bust, two days before Beppo’s arrest.

l: Beppo’s arrest, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Beppo’s arrest followed a crime of violence at Gelder & Co. while the six busts were being made. He was sentenced to a year in prison, during which the busts were distributed across London and he lost track of which one held the pearl.

l: the bust investigation, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: concerns the famous black pearl of the Borgias [traced through the Napoleon busts] The bust investigation links Beppo’s criminal history, the six Napoleon busts, Pietro’s murder, and the missing Borgia pearl. Holmes tracks the busts from Harker’s through the London and Reading locations, ultimately recovering the pearl from the final bust.

l: Beppo’s concealment of the pearl, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: occurs_at Gelder & Co. [inside a wet plaster bust at the factory] Beppo concealed the pearl by making a small hole in one of six soft, wet plaster busts, dropping the jewel inside, and covering the opening. Because the pearl adhered to the wet plaster, shaking the busts would not reveal which one contained it.

l: Hilton Soames, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Hilton Soames is a nervous, excitable tutor, lecturer, and Greek examiner at the College of St. Luke’s, with rooms on the ground floor. He administers an examination whose proofs are tampered with after Bannister leaves a key in his door. With the examination imminent, Soames asks Sherlock Holmes to investigate, identifies three students who use the stair, helps question Bannister and Gilchrist, and is relieved when the attempted theft is explained.

l: Bannister, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Bannister is Hilton Soames’s servant of ten years, a man widely regarded as absolutely honest. Formerly butler to Sir Jabez Gilchrist, he remains loyal to Gilchrist’s son after Sir Jabez is ruined and Bannister serves at the college. When disturbed papers are discovered, Bannister leaves his key in Soames’s door, becomes deeply upset, and is questioned about his movements. Though Holmes and Watson consider him honest, Bannister’s conduct seems puzzling. He first denies that anyone hid in the bedroom, but Holmes reveals the lie. Bannister admits he recognized Gilchrist’s gloves, concealed him, and tried to protect him while urging him not to profit from the theft.

l: Daulat Ras, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Daulat Ras is an Indian student living on the second-floor college staircase near Hilton Soames. Quiet, inscrutable, steady, and methodical, he is strong academically but weak in Greek and prepares for an examination the next day. After visiting Soames to ask about it before the proofs were disturbed, he paces restlessly while studying; Watson suspects him, but Holmes says he may simply be memorizing.

l: Gilchrist, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Gilchrist is a student, fine scholar, and athlete who plays rugby and cricket, excels at hurdling, the long jump, and long-distance jumping, and is tall, lithe, and agile. Poor after his father Sir Jabez Gilchrist’s ruin, he works hard and occupies the lower student room. After seeing examination proofs through Soames’s window, he enters, copies them sheet by sheet, and hides in the bedroom. He confesses, refuses to compete in the scholarship examination, accepts a Rhodesian Police commission, and leaves for South Africa.

l: Miles McLaren, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Miles McLaren is a top-floor student, brilliant when he works but wayward and unprincipled. After a prior card scandal and poor examination preparation, he refuses Holmes entry and abusively appears suspicious to Soames.

l: the three students, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The three students are three men living on successive stories above the tutor’s room, all entered for the examination and possible suspects in the entry into Soames’s room. Holmes investigates their rooms and circumstances, then must choose among them; Daulat Ras is seen pacing, while Gilchrist and Miles McLaren remain unseen.

l: College of St. Luke’s, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: College of St. Luke’s is a college in a great university town, with green-baize and oak doors, employing Hilton Soames while preparing for an examination threatened by a potentially scandalous tampered paper.

l: Cambridge, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: It contains four stationer's shops of consequence and Trinity College, where Jeremy Dixon is located. It is home to the university rugby team and a destination in Godfrey Staunton's disappearance: Holmes and Watson stay there, search nearby villages, and Holmes follows Armstrong's carriage to a lonely cottage.

l: the Fortescue Scholarship, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: has the Greek examination [first day of the examination] The Fortescue Scholarship is the competition for which the confidential Greek examination is being prepared. It is described as valuable, creating a substantial incentive for an unscrupulous candidate to obtain the paper in advance.

l: the Greek examination, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The Greek examination, involving an unseen Thucydides translation passage, is threatened when a candidate may have prepared it in advance. Although the examination proceeds, Gilchrist confesses to attempted theft and copying and is prevented from competing, preserving its fairness.

l: the examination paper, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The examination paper consists of three printer-prepared proof slips containing a Greek translation passage; while Hilton Soames is away, someone moves and apparently copies them, leaving pencil, desk, and clay evidence.

l: the examination scandal, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: threatens College of St. Luke’s [if the examination paper is compromised] The examination scandal concerns the apparent unauthorized access to and copying of the confidential Greek paper. Hilton Soames wants to avoid postponing the examination and exposing the College of St. Luke’s and the university to public disgrace.

l: the intruder, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: tampers_with examination paper [by rummaging among the proofs and copying them] The intruder entered Hilton Soames’s room while the door was accessible through Bannister’s forgotten key. The person moved the papers to the window table, copied them in haste, broke and resharpened a large pencil, and apparently hid in Soames’s bedroom before escaping.

l: the key, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Bannister’s key, left in Hilton Soames’s outer door after he asked about tea, kept the unlocked door open, enabling someone to enter and leave.

l: the examination pencil, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The examination pencil is an unusually large, soft-leaded, dark blue pencil with silver lettering, seldom stocked by stationers. Only about an inch and a half remains, bearing “NN.” It was used and resharpened while copying a paper; Holmes uses its chips to seek a duplicate from four significant town stationers.

l: the black clay, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: contains sawdust [black, doughy or putty-like substance] The black clay is a small, roughly pyramidal, hollowed-out pellet containing specks resembling sawdust. Matching pieces are found on Hilton Soames’s study table and in his bedroom, supporting Holmes’s conclusion that the intruder passed through or concealed himself in the bedroom.

l: Rugby, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_a amateur sport [described as healthy and sound] Rugby is presented as the amateur sport in which Cyril Overton and Godfrey Staunton are prominent. Overton describes Staunton’s abilities in passing, tackling, dribbling, kicking, and organizing the team.

l: foul-mouthed student, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: A student with the worst record among three men becomes Watson's preferred suspect in the dark quadrangle.

l: nervous tutor, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The nervous tutor is mentioned by Holmes as one of the people involved in the problem that he and Watson intend to solve.

l: the investigation, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: An investigation concerns a nervous tutor, Bannister, three enterprising students, and pencil evidence; after a failed duplicate-pencil search, Holmes believes sufficient evidence can build the case.

l: pencil clue, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The pencil clue, described as the best and only final clue, is tested by Holmes through four stationers; none can supply a duplicate, so the search fails and it runs to nothing.

l: the mystery, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The mystery is solved when Holmes determines that Gilchrist entered Soames’s room, handled the proofs, and fled into the bedroom when Soames returned. Bannister’s concealment of Gilchrist is explained by his former service to Gilchrist’s father and his wish to guide the young man toward an honorable decision.

l: the attempted examination-paper theft, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The attempted examination-paper theft involved Gilchrist entering Soames’s unlocked room after seeing examination proofs, copying them sheet by sheet, then abandoning the effort when Soames returned.

l: the examination proofs, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: are_on the central table [in Soames’s room] The examination proofs were on Soames’s central table, where Gilchrist saw them through the window. Gilchrist removed them sheet by sheet to copy them and then left them behind when he fled into the bedroom.

l: the black clay samples, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: come_from the jumping-pit [tenacious black clay] The black clay samples connect the room to the athletic grounds. Holmes finds clay on the table and in the bedroom, then obtains another sample from the jumping-pit, establishing that the clay came from Gilchrist’s athletic practice.

l: the jumping-shoes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: have sharp spikes [several] The jumping-shoes belonged to Gilchrist and had sharp spikes that left a scratch on the table. Clay from the jumping-pit clung to a spike, and the direction of the scratch showed that the shoes were drawn toward the bedroom.

l: the gloves, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: are_left_on the chair [near the window] The gloves were left by Gilchrist on a chair near the window while he copied the proofs. Bannister recognized them and sat on the chair to conceal them from Soames.

l: the examination-paper copying, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_committed_by Gilchrist The examination-paper copying began after Gilchrist confirmed that the papers on Soames’s table were the proofs. He copied them sheet by sheet, but he did not intend to profit from the unfair advantage and wrote that he would not enter the examination.

l: Professor Coram, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Professor Coram is an old, infirm Russian professor and heavy smoker who owns and lives at Yoxley Old Place. A learned man, he works in his study on a manuscript analyzing documents from Coptic monasteries, keeps the bureau key on his watch-chain, and employs Willoughby Smith as secretary and assistant within a self-contained household. When Smith is killed, Coram is ill in bed, says he heard the cry but knows nothing, and proposes accident or suicide while minimizing Smith’s final words. His large meals and composed conduct contrast with the crime. He is ultimately revealed as Sergius, Anna’s husband: he betrayed Anna and the revolutionaries for his life and a reward, hid her diary and Alexis’s letters, and concealed Anna behind a bookcase. After Anna killed his first secretary, Coram helped hide and feed her, while acknowledging that she controls his fate.

l: Willoughby Smith, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Willoughby Smith is a young university graduate who serves as Professor Coram’s secretary and assistant, writing from dictation each morning. He is regarded as decent, quiet, hard-working, and estimable, with no known weakness or enemy, and is a lighter smoker than Coram. At Yoxley Old Place, he catches Anna taking documents from a cupboard. During her escape, she strikes him with an object from the table, fatally stabbing his neck with a sealing-wax knife. Found dying in the study clutching golden pince-nez, he says, “The professor, it was she.”

l: Susan Tarlton, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Susan Tarlton, a country maid serving Professor Coram at Yoxley Old Place, hears Willoughby Smith enter the study, a cry and thud, then finds him wounded and receives his dying statement.

l: Mrs. Marker, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Mrs. Marker, elderly housekeeper at Yoxley Old Place, works for Professor Coram, dusts furniture, is away when the crime occurs, and later finds him agitated in bed.

l: Yoxley Old Place, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Yoxley Old Place is a country house in Kent, seven miles from Chatham and far from the railway. It is Professor Coram’s home and the setting of Willoughby Smith’s murder. The investigation examines its garden path, back door, study, and cocoanut-matted corridors, then reveals a concealed room behind a bookcase, where Anna hides after stealing documents and killing the first secretary until Holmes finds her.

l: Yoxley Old Place murder, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The apparently motiveless Yoxley Old Place murder occurs in the professor's study late one morning; an intruder apparently enters and leaves cautiously by the garden, leaving no clear footprints or motive.

l: death of Willoughby Smith, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Willoughby Smith dies at Yoxley Old Place after a woman searching a wooden bureau stabs him from behind with a small sealing-wax knife, severing his carotid artery. Before dying, he briefly identifies the professor and the female assailant; Holmes concludes she used the knife after Smith caught her.

l: study (Yoxley Old Place), The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Yoxley Old Place’s study contains a large writing-table with open drawers, a locked cupboard, and a fixed wooden bureau, with a back door toward the garden. A suspected woman allegedly searched the table and bureau; Willoughby Smith interrupted her and was fatally stabbed near the bureau, while the sealing-wax knife lay away.

l: Professor Coram’s room, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: contains hidden room behind the bookcase [concealed behind a secret bookcase door] Anna reaches Professor Coram’s room after mistaking one corridor for another while fleeing without her glasses. Coram speaks with her there, agrees to shield her, and hides her behind the bookcase.

l: garden (Yoxley Old Place), The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: contains the garden path The garden is examined as the suspected woman’s route into and out of Yoxley Old Place. Holmes studies the path and the strip of grass beside it, where marks had reportedly been seen.

l: the knife, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The knife is a small old-fashioned sealing-wax knife with an ivory handle and stiff blade, belonging to Professor Coram’s study desk. Found on the carpet beside the wounded Willoughby Smith, it is identified as the weapon. Holmes believes a suspected woman used it to stab Smith; Coram suggests Smith discarded it during a suicide.

l: golden pince-nez, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The golden pince-nez, a gold-mounted, unusually strong pair of spectacles with broken black silk cords, is found in Willoughby Smith’s hand after death and gives Holmes clues to its female owner.

l: bureau (Professor Coram's study), The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: A wooden bureau, apparently the suspected woman’s objective, bears a recent scratch near its keyhole, suggesting someone tried to open it or hastily withdrew its Chubb’s key.

l: murder motive, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: No motive is found for the murder. Stanley Hopkins emphasizes that Willoughby Smith had no known enemy and that nothing appears to have been stolen.

l: Willoughby Smith's dying statement, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Willoughby Smith’s dying statement identifies Professor Coram and implicates a woman; he says, “The professor, it was she,” tries to continue, then dies.

l: Holmes's deductions from the pince-nez, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Holmes’s deductions from a pince-nez identify its wearer as a well-dressed woman with a broad-based nose, close-set eyes, a puckered, peering expression, rounded shoulders, and extremely poor eyesight; worn and replaced cork pads indicate at least two recent optician visits.

l: Anna, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Anna, a severely short-sighted Russian revolutionary and reformer, is married to Professor Coram and imprisoned in Siberia for a limited term. Seeking documents in Coram’s house, she enters through the garden, crosses the corridor, reaches the bureau, and is interrupted by Willoughby Smith. She accidentally kills the first secretary, hides behind the bookcase, gives Holmes a packet intended to save Alexis, recounts her history with Coram, and dies by poison.

l: the police investigation, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: investigates the murder of Willoughby Smith The police investigation finds no recorded stranger arriving or leaving at the station and no unaccounted-for person at local inns or lodgings. Stanley Hopkins investigates reports of a strange woman, while Sherlock Holmes continues examining physical clues at Yoxley Old Place.

l: Willoughby Smith's death, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Willoughby Smith’s death occurred after he confronted a woman in the study. His reported final words, “The professor, it was she,” are disputed by Professor Coram, who claims they were incoherent delirious words.

l: the suicide theory, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Professor Coram suggests that Willoughby Smith may have taken his own life because of hidden troubles or a love affair. He explains the eyeglasses and knife as possible tokens or objects displaced during a suicide, and Sherlock Holmes briefly considers the theory.

l: the bureau key, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The bureau key is kept by Professor Coram on his watch-chain and is identified as a Chubb’s key. Professor Coram later hands it to Sherlock Holmes, who examines it briefly and returns it.

l: the eyeglasses, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The eyeglasses are treated as evidence associated with the suspected woman and with the suicide theory. Children who saw a woman near Chatham reported that she wore either spectacles or eyeglasses.

l: Alexandrian cigarettes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Cigarettes specially prepared by Ionides of Alexandria are supplied to Professor Coram in thousand-count lots; Coram consumes them rapidly, Holmes smokes several, and considers them useful in determining whether he is mistaken.

l: the scratch on the bureau, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The scratch on the bureau begins on the brasswork beside the keyhole and extends about four inches across the varnish. Sherlock Holmes determines that it is recent because the cut brass shines and flakes of varnish remain beside it; he connects it with someone trying to withdraw or use the key.

l: the garden path, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The garden path had no visible marks when examined later, but Stanley Hopkins says that tracks had been clear on the narrow grass margin the previous day. Holmes reasons that the suspected woman may have carefully walked on the grass to avoid leaving marks on the path or flower-bed.

l: Alexis, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Alexis, Anna’s noble and loving fellow revolutionary and friend, is convicted after Coram tries to swear away his life, sent to Siberia to work in a salt mine, while Anna seeks his release through recovered papers.

l: the Brotherhood, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_a revolutionary organization [Russian] The Brotherhood was the revolutionary organization to which Anna, Coram, and their companions belonged. Anna says it would have sought justice against Coram if it had learned where he was living.

l: Siberia, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: contains Alexis’s imprisonment in Siberia Siberia is where Anna was imprisoned for a limited term after the revolutionary arrests. Alexis was also sent there as a convict and is working in a salt mine when Anna tells her story.

l: Russian Embassy, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: receives the packet for the Russian Embassy [for delivery to the Russian government] Anna entrusts Holmes with a packet and asks him to deliver it to the Russian Embassy so that Alexis may be saved. Holmes and Watson travel toward the Russian Embassy with the packet.

l: Professor Coram’s study, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Anna enters Professor Coram’s study to obtain documents from the cupboard. She has a key made from an impression supplied by an agent, but the first secretary catches her while she is locking the cupboard.

l: hidden room behind the bookcase, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: conceals Anna The hidden room behind the bookcase is an old hiding-place known only to Professor Coram. Anna stays there while Coram supplies her with part of his meals, and Holmes identifies it as her hiding-place.

l: the murder of the first secretary, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_caused_by Anna’s theft of the documents [during Anna’s escape] Anna kills the first secretary accidentally while trying to escape after he seizes her. She says she did not know that the object she grabbed from the table was a knife and struck only to make him release her.

l: Anna’s theft of the documents, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: targets the documents in Professor Coram’s bureau Anna steals documents from the cupboard in Professor Coram’s study. She seeks them because they include material needed to help Alexis and because Coram would not willingly surrender them.

l: the betrayal of Anna and the revolutionaries, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_committed_by Professor Coram [to save his own life and gain a reward] Coram betrayed Anna and their fellow revolutionaries after a police officer was killed, giving evidence to save his own life and earn a reward. His confession led to arrests, executions, imprisonment in Siberia, and Alexis’s conviction.

l: Alexis’s imprisonment in Siberia, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_caused_by the betrayal of Anna and the revolutionaries Alexis is sent as a convict to Siberia after Coram attempts to implicate him. At the time of Anna’s confession, Alexis works as a slave in a salt mine, and Anna seeks his release.

l: Holmes’s investigation, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Holmes’s investigation uses Anna’s pince-nez to conclude she probably remained in the house, then examines the room, tests the floor with cigarette ash, notes Coram’s increased food consumption, and identifies a secret bookcase door as her likely hiding-place.

l: the escape and concealment of Anna, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: After the secretary falls, Anna runs through the wrong corridor, reaches Coram’s room, and is concealed by Coram behind the bookcase. She remains there while the police search the house and plans to leave after they depart.

l: Anna’s suicide by poison, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Anna takes poison before leaving the hidden room. Holmes removes the poison phial from her hand, but she says it is too late and dies after charging him to remember the packet.

l: Anna’s diary, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Anna’s diary records her feelings toward Alexis and the views held by the revolutionaries from day to day. Coram found and kept it, and Anna seeks to recover it because it could help secure Alexis’s release.

l: Alexis’s letters, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Alexis’s letters argued against revolutionary violence and could have helped save him. Coram found and kept them, while Anna tries to recover them so they can be sent to the Russian government.

l: the packet for the Russian Embassy, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Anna gives Holmes a small packet containing the material that will save Alexis. She asks him to deliver it to the Russian Embassy, and Holmes takes it with him.

l: pince-nez, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: belongs_to Anna The pince-nez belong to Anna and are found after the dying secretary seizes them. Holmes infers from their strength that Anna is extremely short-sighted and helpless without them, making an outdoor escape unlikely.

l: the poison phial, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The poison phial is in Anna’s hand when she reveals that she has taken poison. Holmes bounds across the room and wrenches it from her, but she has already taken a fatal dose.

l: the secret bookcase door, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: conceals hidden room behind the bookcase The secret bookcase door swings on a hinge and opens into Anna’s hiding-place. Holmes suspects it because one bookcase is left clear while books are piled elsewhere, and the door is revealed when Anna rushes out.

l: the cigarette-box ash traces, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: reveal the escape and concealment of Anna [by showing movement before the bookcase] Holmes drops cigarette ash in front of the suspected bookcase to track movement across the floor. After the cigarette-box is upset, the traces show that Anna has emerged from her retreat while the investigators were absent.

l: the documents in Professor Coram’s bureau, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The documents are kept in a cupboard or bureau in Professor Coram’s study. Anna uses a key made from an impression obtained by her detective agent and steals the papers while seeking evidence that will help Alexis.

l: the case of the hidden woman, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_solved_by Sherlock Holmes The case concerns Anna’s theft of documents, the murder of the first secretary, and her concealment inside Professor Coram’s house. Holmes resolves it by connecting the pince-nez, the similar corridors, Coram’s increased food consumption, and the cigarette ash before exposing Anna behind the bookcase.

l: Overton, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Cyril Overton is Cambridge University’s rugby captain and an England reserve. When indispensable teammate Godfrey Staunton disappears, Overton asks Sherlock Holmes to investigate, stresses Staunton’s importance, and consults the other players.

l: Godfrey Staunton, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Godfrey Staunton is an orphaned, healthy international rugby player: Cambridge’s leading three-quarter, also playing for Blackheath, with five Internationals. Nephew and heir of Lord Mount-James, he depends on concealing his secret marriage. Pale and troubled, he leaves Bentley’s private hotel with a bearded stranger, abandons his belongings, sends an urgent telegram to his intimate friend Dr. Leslie Armstrong, and disappears before the Cambridge–Oxford match. He is later found at a lonely cottage, kneeling beside his dead wife and overwhelmed by grief. His marriage to his former London landlady’s daughter had prevented him from withdrawing from the match without revealing it.

l: Lord Mount-James, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Lord Mount-James, Godfrey Staunton’s uncle, nearest relative, and presumed heir-giver, is a miser among England’s richest men. He first refuses to fund Staunton’s search, then becomes alarmed when kidnapping is linked to his wealth.

l: the bearded stranger, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: A rough, grizzled, pale-faced man about fifty delivers Godfrey Staunton a note at Bentley’s private hotel, appears agitated, discusses “time,” and leaves with Staunton toward the Strand.

l: the hotel porter, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Bentley’s private hotel porter observes a bearded stranger, reports Staunton’s reaction and departure, and tells Holmes about Staunton’s telegram and reply.

l: Cambridge University rugby team, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: plays_against Oxford rugby team [in the Cambridge–Oxford rugby match] The Cambridge University rugby team is captained by Cyril Overton and is preparing to play Oxford. Its prospects are seriously damaged by the disappearance of Godfrey Staunton, whom Overton regards as the team’s essential three-quarter.

l: Oxford rugby team, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: plays_against Cambridge University rugby team [in the Cambridge–Oxford rugby match] The Oxford rugby team is scheduled to play Cambridge University in the important match the day after Staunton disappears. Its players are mentioned as the opponents against whom Cambridge may be unable to compete effectively without Staunton.

l: Bentley’s private hotel, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: accommodates Cambridge University rugby team [during the team’s visit to London] Bentley’s private hotel is where the Cambridge University rugby team stays before the match. Godfrey Staunton receives the note there, leaves with the bearded stranger, and is found to have abandoned his room without sleeping in his bed.

l: telegram, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: A telegram sent to Sherlock Holmes asks him to await Cyril Overton because the team’s right wing three-quarter is missing and indispensable the next day. Another telegram sent by Staunton contains an incomplete appeal for help.

l: Staunton's telegram, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Staunton’s telegram, sent by Godfrey Staunton from London to Dr. Leslie Armstrong at six-fifteen the previous evening, was urgently addressed without a name and asked for help against danger: “Stand by us for God’s sake!” Sent within hours of Staunton’s disappearance, it suggests that he and another person sought protection; Armstrong denies receiving it.

l: the note for Godfrey Staunton, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The note for Godfrey Staunton is delivered by the bearded stranger at Bentley’s private hotel. Reading it causes Staunton to collapse back in his chair, after which he leaves with the stranger.

l: Godfrey Staunton's room, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: contains Staunton's papers [after Staunton’s disappearance] Godfrey Staunton’s room at Bentley’s private hotel contains his untouched belongings and an unslept-in bed after his disappearance. Holmes searches the room, examines the papers, and finds an impression of Staunton’s telegram on the blotting-paper.

l: blotting-paper message, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: records Stand by us for God’s sake [as the surviving end of Staunton’s telegram] The blotting-paper message preserves the reverse impression of part of Staunton’s telegram. Holmes reads the surviving words as “Stand by us for God’s sake!” and treats them as the principal clue in the investigation.

l: the Cambridge–Oxford rugby match, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The Cambridge–Oxford rugby match, scheduled for the day after Godfrey Staunton disappears, is significant because his presence seems essential to Cambridge. Oxford wins by a goal and two tries; Cambridge, the Light Blues, loses partly because Staunton’s skill is greatly missed.

l: Godfrey Staunton's disappearance, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Godfrey Staunton disappears in London on the eve of the Cambridge–Oxford rugby match after leaving his hotel, prompting an urgent telegram and Sherlock Holmes’s investigation. Holmes considers kidnapping and links Dr. Leslie Armstrong’s journeys and reaction to the case.

l: kidnapping, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: may_seek ransom [by abducting Godfrey Staunton] Kidnapping is considered by Holmes as one possible explanation for Staunton’s disappearance. He suggests to Lord Mount-James that criminals might hold Staunton to obtain information about the old man’s house, habits, and treasure.

l: Godfrey Staunton's inheritance, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_at_risk_from Godfrey Staunton's secret marriage [the marriage would end it if disclosed] Godfrey Staunton is described as Lord Mount-James’s heir, although Lord Mount-James has never given him money. The inheritance provides a possible financial motive for Staunton’s disappearance, but no definite connection is established in this unit.

l: Dr. Leslie Armstrong, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Dr. Leslie Armstrong is a formidable, grim, ascetic, self-contained doctor: a medical-school head, lecturer, consultant, and European-reputation thinker. He avoids general practice, writes a treatise rather than converse with Holmes, owns a house and a carriage, and makes long daily journeys while guarding against followers. Though he dislikes Holmes’s profession, he knows and loves his intimate friend Godfrey Staunton and helps conceal Staunton’s secret marriage to protect his inheritance. Initially Armstrong denies knowledge of Staunton’s disappearance, angrily expels Holmes and Watson, detects their surveillance, and attempts to mislead them with a circuitous route. He ultimately returns to the cottage, explains the marriage and the wife’s illness, and accepts Holmes’s promise of confidentiality.

l: the old university city, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: contains the university The old university city is reached after dark by Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson. Holmes describes it as an inhospitable town, and its flat surrounding countryside makes it difficult to follow or conceal oneself.

l: Dr. Armstrong's daily journeys, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: use the brougham [with a pair of greys] Dr. Armstrong's daily journeys are made by carriage for ten or twelve miles, once or sometimes twice a day. Sherlock Holmes follows one journey but loses the carriage when Armstrong takes a side road, and Armstrong later returns to his house after detecting the pursuit.

l: the case, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: concerns Godfrey Staunton's disappearance The case concerns Godfrey Staunton's disappearance and Dr. Leslie Armstrong's possible knowledge of it. Holmes remains in the old university city because leaving would mean abandoning the case, and he refuses to leave the matter unresolved.

l: the receipted bill, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: records_payment thirteen guineas [from Godfrey Staunton to Dr. Leslie Armstrong last month] The receipted bill shows that Godfrey Staunton paid thirteen guineas to Dr. Leslie Armstrong the previous month. Sherlock Holmes finds it among Staunton's papers and uses it to challenge Armstrong, who refuses to explain it.

l: the inn, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The inn opposite Dr. Armstrong's house lodges Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson during the investigation; Holmes returns exhausted, then uses its proximity to a bicycle shop to follow Armstrong's carriage.

l: Godfrey Staunton's wife, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Godfrey Staunton's wife is a young, beautiful, good, and intelligent woman. She suffers a dangerous, virulent consumption and, after Staunton returns from the rugby match, is found dead at the lonely cottage.

l: the lonely cottage, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: A private countryside residence near Cambridge where Godfrey Staunton secretly lives with his wife; Dr. Armstrong conceals their marriage, and Holmes and Watson find Staunton grieving beside her body.

l: Pompey, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Pompey, Sherlock Holmes’s squat white-and-tan draghound, uses his strong scenting ability to follow an aniseed-marked carriage trail through deception, leading Holmes and Watson to a lonely cottage.

l: Godfrey Staunton's secret marriage, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Godfrey Staunton secretly married his London landlady's daughter to protect his inheritance from Lord Mount-James. Dr. Leslie Armstrong and a cottage servant privately knew, until an investigation reached the cottage.

l: Godfrey Staunton's wife's illness, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Staunton’s wife develops a dangerous, ultimately fatal consumption of the most virulent kind, prompting Staunton to leave the rugby match and return to the cottage frenzied.

l: Godfrey Staunton's wife's death, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: ends Godfrey Staunton's wife's sufferings [after her illness] Staunton’s wife dies at the lonely cottage, ending her suffering. Staunton remains beside her in overwhelming grief until Holmes and Watson arrive.

l: Sir Eustace Brackenstall, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Sir Eustace Brackenstall, a baronet married to Lady Brackenstall, is a confirmed drunkard whose violent episodes abuse her. In the dining room, he is found dead with a severe head injury after allegedly entering with his blackthorn cudgel and being struck by a burglar with his poker.

l: Lady Brackenstall, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Lady Brackenstall is a woman from South Australia, married for about a year to Sir Eustace Brackenstall in an unhappy and abusive marriage. After his death at Abbey Grange, she is injured over one eye and on her arm. She tells Sherlock Holmes and Inspector Stanley Hopkins that three burglars attacked her, tied and gagged her, killed Sir Eustace, drank wine, stole silver, and escaped through a French window. Holmes concludes that this burglary account was fabricated, that she was tied to the chair after Sir Eustace’s death, and that she is protecting the real criminal. The false story, corroborated by the maid, is intended to shield that person from prosecution, while Captain Crocker seeks to protect her if possible.

l: Theresa Wright, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Theresa Wright is Lady Brackenstall’s lifelong, devoted maid, nurse, and attendant, who came with her from Australia. Stern and suspicious, she hates Sir Eustace, her late employer, for abusing Lady Brackenstall and having once thrown a decanter at her. She reports finding Lady Brackenstall bound and Sir Eustace dead after seeing three men near the lodge gate, supports her mistress’s account, angrily rejects Holmes’s accusation of lying, and assists Captain Crocker in staging a supposed burglary. She was formerly Mary Fraser’s attendant and protector.

l: the Lewisham gang, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The Lewisham gang, identified by Inspector Stanley Hopkins as the Randall family, father and two sons, is a burglary gang. After a substantial burglary at Sydenham, it is suspected of the Abbey Grange burglary and killing because it matches Lady Brackenstall’s description. Its arrest in New York proves it could not have committed the Kent murder that night.

l: Abbey Grange, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Abbey Grange is the Brackenstalls’ large country house in Marsham, Kent, home of Sir Eustace Brackenstall. It has an old central block, a modern wing, and a dining-room whose French window opens onto the lawn. After dinner, Captain Crocker encounters Mary Fraser there, kills Sir Eustace, and helps stage an apparent burglary with a cut bell rope, Mary tied to a chair, and missing silver. Holmes later examines the dining-room evidence.

l: the murder of Lady Brackenstall's husband, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: At Abbey Grange, Sir Eustace Brackenstall is violently killed in the dining-room by a poker blow to the head. Lady Brackenstall blames three burglars, but Holmes finds the burglary story fabricated: one powerful, agile man killed Sir Eustace, and Lady Brackenstall was tied to her chair afterward to stage the scene.

l: the burglary at Abbey Grange, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The Abbey Grange burglary allegedly involves three men entering through the dining-room French window, binding Lady Brackenstall, killing Sir Eustace Brackenstall, taking silver plate, and drinking wine. They close the window on leaving; frozen ground yields no clear tracks. Inspector Stanley Hopkins attributes it to the Lewisham gang.

l: the investigation, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The investigation concerns the murder of Sir Eustace Brackenstall. Inspector Stanley Hopkins asks Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson for help; Holmes examines witnesses, the room, physical evidence, and wine glasses. What first seems clear to Hopkins becomes doubtful, and Holmes delays decisive legal action while seeking more information.

l: the poker, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_used_to_kill Sir Eustace Brackenstall The blackthorn poker is found bent into a curve beside Sir Eustace Brackenstall’s body, and the damage to it is consistent with the force of the blow that injured his head. Lady Brackenstall says that an elderly burglar picked it from the grate and used it to strike Sir Eustace.

l: the bell-rope, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The bell-rope is attached to the dining-room and, at its upper end, to the bell wire. It was cut three inches from the top, leaving a clean upper end and frayed lower end. Holmes concludes a tall, strong man cut it from the mantelpiece without ringing the kitchen bell.

l: the wine bottle, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The wine bottle, two-thirds full and of an uncommon vintage, was opened with a short pocket screw rather than the drawer’s large corkscrew. The screw was driven in three times without piercing the cork, leading Holmes to infer a multiplex knife.

l: the wine glasses, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Three wine glasses, each tinged with wine, are found in the dining-room. Holmes is troubled that only one contains beeswing despite a claim that three men drank. He concludes two glasses were used and their dregs poured into a third to suggest three drinkers.

l: the stolen silver, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The stolen silver, about half a dozen articles from Abbey Grange’s sideboard, is taken in a supposed burglary and hidden beneath ice at the park pond. Later found at the bottom, it may have been a blind for people who did not want it.

l: Captain Crocker, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Captain Crocker is a large, strong, active, sunburned sailor and first officer of the Rock of Gibraltar when he meets Mary Fraser, whom he loves devotedly without return for much of their relationship. On a later voyage he is promoted first officer and is due to depart. After witnessing Mary’s husband assault her, Crocker kills him with a poker. He helps Mary and Theresa Wright disguise the death as a burglary by cutting and tying the bell-rope and disposing of silver in a pond. He confesses fully, refuses to flee without Mary, and is acquitted in Holmes’s informal trial.

l: the three burglars, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: are_imaginary burglars in the account [according to Holmes's suspicion] The three burglars described by Lady Brackenstall are presented as having entered early, attacked her, murdered her husband, taken limited silver, drunk wine, and escaped. Holmes finds the behavior improbable and concludes that the three men were imaginary figures in a fabricated account.

l: the maid, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: corroborates Lady Brackenstall [in the burglary account] The maid supports Lady Brackenstall’s account of the three burglars and helps treat the bruise on her mistress’s brow. Holmes considers her corroboration part of the deliberate falsehood, and she refuses to provide any different information.

l: the park pond, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: contains the stolen silver [at the bottom beneath the ice] The park pond, which is frozen except for a hole left for a swan, becomes the hiding place for the stolen silver. Holmes directs Hopkins to examine it, and the silver is recovered from the water.

l: the wooden bracket, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: supports the bell-rope [used as a foothold] The wooden bracket bears an impression in the dust. Holmes determines that the suspected man placed his knee on it to reach the bell-rope and cut it.

l: the oaken chair, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: has_blood_on the seat [showing Lady Brackenstall was placed there after the death] The oaken chair has a blood mark on its seat. Holmes uses this evidence to conclude that Lady Brackenstall was not sitting there during the killing but was placed in the chair afterward.

l: the fabricated burglary story, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Lady Brackenstall, supported by the maid, tells an invented account of three burglars. Holmes concludes that Captain Crocker and Theresa Wright staged it to conceal a murder and protect the real criminal.

l: Mary Fraser's husband, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Mary Fraser’s husband is described as a drunken, violent man who physically and verbally abuses Mary Fraser, fights Captain Crocker, and is killed by Crocker with a poker.

l: the murder of Mary Fraser's husband, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_presented_as self-defense [subject to determination by a British jury] The murder occurs when Captain Crocker intervenes after Mary Fraser's husband strikes her. Crocker says the fight was between the two men and that he killed the husband because it was his life or Crocker's, and because he could not leave Mary in the husband's power.

l: Captain Crocker's account of the murder, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_true the whole truth [according to Captain Crocker and Holmes] Captain Crocker recounts meeting Mary Fraser during a voyage, learning of her unhappy marriage, and entering the Abbey Grange to see her before leaving on another voyage. He says Mary Fraser's husband attacked her, after which Crocker killed him, helped give Mary wine, cut the bell rope, tied Mary to her chair, scattered the appearance of a robbery, and discarded the silver in a pond.

l: the acquittal of Captain Crocker, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Sherlock Holmes informally judges Captain Crocker, with Dr. Watson as jury; Watson finds him not guilty, Holmes acquits him, and warns that the law may still claim another victim.

l: self-defense, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Sherlock Holmes acknowledges that Captain Crocker acted under extreme provocation and may have acted legitimately in defense of his own life. He says that whether the killing legally qualifies as self-defense would ordinarily be decided by a British jury.

l: the Prime Minister, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The Prime Minister, Lord Bellinger, is a former twice Premier of Britain and head of government. With Trelawney Hope, he seeks Sherlock Holmes’s help over a missing letter whose disclosure could cause European complications and war. Later, while lunching with Hope, he recognizes the recovered document and congratulates him.

l: Trelawney Hope, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Trelawney Hope is the Secretary for European Affairs, a rising statesman who lives at Whitehall Terrace with his wife, Lady Hilda Trelawney Hope. He keeps political matters from her and owns a locked despatch-box. A foreign letter vanishes from that box after he sees it there before dinner, threatening his political career and public consequences. Later, returning home while Holmes is with Lady Hilda, he opens the box, finds the document intact, and reacts with relief and astonishment.

l: Eduardo Lucas, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Eduardo Lucas is a thirty-four-year-old unmarried man living at 16 Godolphin Street, well known in society as an amateur tenor, linguist, student of international politics, and intimate associate of leading politicians. Beneath this public identity, he is an international spy and secret agent, one of three capable of handling a stolen political letter, and lives a double life as Henri Fournaye in London and Paris. He has superficial relationships with women and possesses Lady Hilda’s indiscreet letter, using it to compel her to take a specified document from her husband’s despatch-box. After she delivers the document at his house, Lucas hides it beneath a drugget in his room. He is then stabbed and murdered there. His papers reveal gossip, letters, and political connections but no clear motive for the killing, leaving him identified chiefly as the victim of the murder of Eduardo Lucas.

l: the foreign potentate, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: A foreign ruler, ruffled by recent Colonial developments in Britain, hurriedly writes a missing letter without his Ministers' knowledge; after it disappears, he receives a cipher telegram about the loss.

l: the narrator, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_a friend and chronicler of Sherlock Holmes The narrator recounts the meeting at Baker Street and explains why the account of the case must remain vague in certain details. He identifies the murder of Eduardo Lucas in the morning newspaper.

l: Lady Hilda Trelawney Hope, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Lady Hilda Trelawney Hope, the Duke of Belminster’s youngest daughter and Trelawney Hope’s wife, lives at the Hope residence and fears damage to her husband’s political career. Before marriage she wrote an indiscreet letter, which Eduardo Lucas uses to blackmail her. Secretly visiting Sherlock Holmes, she seeks information about a stolen political paper while concealing her motive. She steals the document from her husband’s despatch-box with a duplicate key to recover the letter, initially denies it, then confesses to Holmes, gives him the document, and returns it, fearing her husband’s discovery.

l: the international spies and secret agents, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: International spies and secret agents are independent operators whose embassy relations are often strained. Holmes says a stolen letter may go to them, naming Oberstein, La Rothiere, and Eduardo Lucas as leading professionals.

l: Whitehall Terrace, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Whitehall Terrace is the location of Trelawney Hope's house, where a letter was kept overnight in a locked despatch-box in his bedroom. It is central to a political incident Holmes and Watson know about, linked by Holmes to Lucas's murder. After leaving the murder scene, Holmes and Watson go there to bring the matter to a head.

l: Godolphin Street, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Godolphin Street is an old-fashioned, secluded row of eighteenth-century houses in Westminster, near Whitehall Terrace. It contains Eduardo Lucas’s London house at number 16, including a carpet hiding-place in his room. Lady Hilda brings Lucas a political document there in exchange for her letter, and he hides it when someone approaches. Later Lucas is found murdered there; a woman thought to be Mme. Fournaye is seen watching the house that night.

l: the letter, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: A secret diplomatic communication from a foreign potentate, addressed to Trelawney Hope and stored in a locked despatch-box. Containing provocative phrases about recent Colonial developments, it disappears by morning; publication could provoke public ferment, European complications, and war.

l: despatch-box (Trelawney Hope's), The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Trelawney Hope’s locked despatch-box, kept in his bedroom at Whitehall Terrace, holds official papers including a political document and letter. Hope opens it while dressing and later finds the document missing. Lady Hilda used a duplicate key; Holmes returns the document before Hope and the Prime Minister inspect the box.

l: Lady Hilda's theft of the political document, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: Lady Hilda’s theft is an internationally consequential removal of a political document, potentially leading to war. To recover her indiscreet letter and prevent her husband from seeing it, she takes an impression of his key, obtains a duplicate from Eduardo Lucas, opens the despatch-box, and removes the paper between 7:30 and 11:30 that evening. Holmes initially suspects it was quickly passed to an international agent, while the incident is linked to Lucas’s death.

l: the publication of the letter, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: could_cause war [through a breach between Britain and the foreign potentate's country] The publication of the letter could reveal provocative remarks by the foreign potentate and produce a dangerous state of feeling in Britain. The statesmen believe it could lead to war and say that enemies of the potentate would benefit from making it public.

l: war, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: War is a possible European conflict that statesmen fear could follow publication of a letter and involve Britain within a week. Though Holmes first advises preparing for war, believing the document lost, he later says tact and management will prevent any war; Europe shows no trouble.

l: the murder of Eduardo Lucas, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The murder of Eduardo Lucas is a wilful killing at Lucas's house, 16 Godolphin Street, on the night before the Baker Street meeting, during the same hours as the Whitehall Terrace political incident. Lucas is stabbed instantly through the heart with a curved Indian dagger in the room where he is killed. A coroner's jury calls it murder. Police attribute it to Mme. Henri Fournaye after a jealous struggle, but Holmes regards the timing and Lucas's possible possession of the letter as evidence of a wider connection and continues investigating.

l: the European political situation, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_a armed balance of power [Britain holds the balance] The European political situation is portrayed as unstable because Europe is an armed camp divided between two military confederacies. Britain holds the balance, so a conflict between Britain and one side would assure the supremacy of the other.

l: 16 Godolphin Street, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: 16 Godolphin Street in Westminster is a small but select mansion where Police-constable Barrett finds its door ajar, a disordered room, and Eduardo Lucas stabbed dead.

l: the Lucas residence (16 Godolphin Street), The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The Lucas residence, inhabited by Eduardo Lucas with Mrs. Pringle and Mitton, is found disordered after his murder; valuables remain, indicating robbery was not the motive.

l: the stolen political paper, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The stolen political paper is an immensely important, politically sensitive document kept in Trelawney Hope’s despatch-box. Its disappearance during the Whitehall Terrace incident threatens terrible public consequences, though Lady Hilda does not understand them and Holmes will not explain. Lady Hilda takes it and gives it to Eduardo Lucas; Holmes recovers it, restores it secretly, and it is found intact.

l: political consequences of the document, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The political consequences of the document are central to a secret involving Lady Hilda Trelawney Hope and her husband. He withholds politics even from his wife, and Holmes cannot disclose the facts because of professional secrecy. Lady Hilda takes the document without understanding its stakes, but it is recovered before public exposure, allowing Holmes to assure the Prime Minister that no danger remains.

l: Lady Hilda's visit to Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_kept_secret_from Lady Hilda Trelawney Hope's husband [at Lady Hilda’s request] Lady Hilda's visit is made secretly, and she asks Holmes not to tell her husband about it. She seeks information about the stolen paper and its consequences, then leaves after Holmes declines to disclose more; afterward, Holmes questions whether her stated motive was genuine.

l: Mme. Henri Fournaye, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: A Creole woman, wife of Eduardo Lucas, living in a small Paris villa, was reportedly permanently and dangerously insane after returning from London. Past jealousy frenzies led Paris police to connect her with Lucas’s death and conjecture she murdered him.

l: Paris, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: contains Rue Austerlitz Paris is where Mme. Henri Fournaye lives and where the police discover her insanity and connection to Eduardo Lucas. Holmes considers searching her house there but fears arousing the suspicions of the French police.

l: the European catastrophe, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_prevented war [as anticipated by Holmes] The European catastrophe is the danger Holmes is trying to prevent by tracing the missing letter. He tells Dr. John Watson that the murder is only a minor incident compared with this larger task.

l: the missing letter, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The missing letter's disappearance is tied to the European catastrophe; it remains unaccounted for and absent from Eduardo Lucas's papers. Holmes considers receipt by Lucas, carriage by Mme. Fournaye to Paris, or concealment.

l: the room where Lucas was killed, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The room where Lucas was killed contains a central drugget with an irregular bloodstain, weapons over the fireplace, and a writing desk in the window. Holmes searches beneath the drugget, finds a concealed floor cavity, and discovers it is empty.

l: the concealed floor cavity, The Return of Sherlock Holmes
s: The concealed floor cavity is hidden beneath one of the square wooden floor sections under the drugget. Holmes opens it during a brief distraction and finds nothing inside.

l: carpet hiding-place (Eduardo Lucas's room), The Return of Sherlock Holmes
